The area of one loop of the polar curve [MATH: r=\sin\left( 2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4} \right)] (shown above) is given by the integral
[MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/8}^{3\pi/8} \sin^2\left(2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \:\textrm{d}\theta.]
Find an integral that represents the total area bounded by the polar curve.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The given polar curve is the polar rose with [MATH: 2 \cdot 2=4] petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is

[MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/8}^{3\pi/8} \sin^2\left(2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \:\textrm{d}\theta.]

Therefore, the total area bounded by the polar curve is [MATH: A_{\textrm{total}}=4\cdot A = 2 \int_{-\pi/8}^{3\pi/8} \sin^2\left(2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \:\textrm{d}\theta.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we want to find the interval for [MATH: \theta] that corresponds to the first petal. Since the curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin, we want to find the values of [MATH: \theta] for which [MATH: r=0], or [MATH: \sin(7\theta) = 0.]

This gives us two solutions for [MATH: 7\theta \in [0,2\pi)\mathbin{:}] [MATH: 7\theta = 0, \pi \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \theta=0,\dfrac{\pi}{7}.]

As a result, the first petal is traversed for [MATH: 0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{7}.]

Since there are [MATH: 7] petals, the total area bounded by the polar curve can be calculated as follows:

[MATH: A_{total}|= 7 ⋅ A_{petal}; = 7 ⋅ (1)/(2)∫_{0}^{π/7}\sin^{2} (7θ)dθ; = (7)/(2) ⋅ (1)/(2)∫_{0}^{π/7}(1 − \cos (14θ))dθ; = (7)/(4)(θ − (1)/(14)\sin (14θ))|_{0}^{π/7}; = (7)/(4)[((π)/(7) − (1)/(14)\sin (2π)) − (0 − (1)/(14)\sin (0))]; = (7)/(4)((π)/(7) − 0); = (π)/(4)]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that the area of one loop of the polar curve [MATH: r=\sin(5\theta)] (shown above) is given by the integral
[MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi/5} \sin^2(5\theta) \:\textrm{d}\theta.]

Content:
How can we find the total area bounded by the curve?

Content:
One method is to count the number of petals and multiply the area of one petal by the total number of petals. In our case, we have [MATH: 5] petals in total, and so the total area bounded by the polar curve is

Content:
[MATH: A_\textrm{total}=5A = \dfrac{5}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi/5} \sin^2(5\theta) \:\textrm{d}\theta.]

Item 5 — Example: Finding the Total Area Bounded by a Single Polar Curve

Find the total area bounded by the polar curve [MATH: r=\sin(7\theta),] shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/aab0ecf46c3a16b846558374613d2bb6]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we want to find the interval for [MATH: \theta] that corresponds to the first petal. Since the curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin, we want to find the values of [MATH: \theta] for which [MATH: r=0], or
[MATH: \sin(7\theta) = 0.]

This gives us two solutions for [MATH: 7\theta \in [0,2\pi)\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: 7\theta = 0, \pi \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \theta=0,\dfrac{\pi}{7}.]

As a result, the first petal is traversed for [MATH: 0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{7}.]

[IMG: /graphics/aa774fe923123c59b095cbfa7a728461]

Since there are [MATH: 7] petals, the total area bounded by the polar curve can be calculated as follows:

[MATH: A_{total}|= 7 ⋅ A_{petal}; = 7 ⋅ (1)/(2)∫_{0}^{π/7}\sin^{2} (7θ)dθ; = (7)/(2) ⋅ (1)/(2)∫_{0}^{π/7}(1 − \cos (14θ))dθ; = (7)/(4)(θ − (1)/(14)\sin (14θ))|_{0}^{π/7}; = (7)/(4)[((π)/(7) − (1)/(14)\sin (2π)) − (0 − (1)/(14)\sin (0))]; = (7)/(4)((π)/(7) − 0); = (π)/(4)]
